verifications.claim: An annual flu shot is recommended for everyone 6 months and older.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine every season (R3); CDC recommends everyone 6 months and older get vaccinated every flu season (R7); Annual flu vaccines are available... for people age 6 months and older (R9)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple CDC and official sources directly state the recommendation for everyone 6 months and older annually.

verifications.claim: An annual flu shot is ideally recommended by the end of October.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: It’s generally recommended that people get a flu vaccine by the end of October (R2); ideally by the end of October (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Direct statements from reliable sources specify 'by the end of October' as ideal.

verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: get a flu vaccine every year (R3); Each year a new flu vaccine is made (R7); New flu vaccines are released every year (R9)
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly confirm yearly updates due to changing viruses.

verifications.claim: The 2025-26 flu season features trivalent vaccines.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: Flu shots are now available for the 2025-2026 season (R1); For 2025-2026 flu season (R3); For the 2025-26 influenza season, all flu vaccines... are trivalent (R5); This 2025-2026 flu season you can get a trivalent flu shot (R8)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources confirm trivalent vaccines specifically for 2025-26 season.

verifications.claim: Trivalent vaccines guard against three main virus strains.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: protect against three influenza viruses (R3); Trivalent flu vaccines protect against three different main groups of influenza Type A and B viruses (R5)

verifications.claim: It takes about two weeks for antibodies to develop after flu vaccination.
verifications.label: CLEAR

verifications.reasoning: Precise timeframe stated in CDC sources.
